Temperature history · Batch identity · Required action

THE PROBLEM IN CONTEXT

A cold delivery can hide a warm journey.

Cold-chain failure occurs when seafood experiences unsuitable temperature conditions during harvest, processing, storage or distribution. Monitoring failure occurs when those conditions are missed, recorded inaccurately or detected without an effective response. Both matter at manufacturing handovers: receiving, filleting, packing and dispatch (FSANZ, 2006; FDA, 2022).

35%global harvest lost or wasted

FAO’s 2020 fisheries and aquaculture overview reports this broad estimate. It includes losses and waste across the value chain from multiple causes. It is not the proportion caused by cold-chain failure, and it is not a measured rate for an Australian processor (FAO, 2020).

For a particular factory, investigate the actual causes and kilograms lost before estimating what better temperature control could prevent.

Safety and trust

Product-specific hazards can develop during unsuitable handling. For histamine-forming fish, later cooking cannot undo histamine formation. A loss of control therefore requires a safety assessment, even when seafood looks acceptable (FDA, 2022).

Quality and income

Shorter remaining quality life can reduce the selling window and lead to rejection or lower-value use. The manufacturing objective is to preserve usable quality while meeting safety controls (Huss, 1995).

Resources and food supply

Preventable disposal wastes resources invested in harvesting, processing and transport. Refrigeration also consumes energy and can contribute emissions through refrigerant leakage, so evaluate cooling and avoided loss together (UNEP & FAO, 2022).

WHY THE ISSUE MATTERS

Cooling slows change. It does not reset freshness.

Microorganisms

Spoilage organisms produce compounds affecting odour and flavour. In some marine fish, bacterial conversion of TMAO to TMA contributes to fishy odours.

Huss, 1995

Natural enzymes

The fish’s own enzymes change tissues after death. Their contribution varies by species and storage conditions.

Huss, 1995

Oxidation and frozen change

Fat oxidation can cause rancid flavours. Freezing still permits quality changes involving proteins, fats and moisture over storage.

Huss, 1995; Johnston et al., 1994
Quality and safety are different. Tuna may develop histamine through bacterial activity; cooking and freezing do not remove it once formed. Reduced-oxygen seafood packaging needs assessment of botulinum toxin risk. A normal smell is not proof of safety. FDA, 2022, Chapters 3, 6, 7 and 13

TEMPERATURE × TIME

How much does a few degrees matter?

Some spoilage bacteria can grow at refrigeration temperatures: these are called psychrotrophic organisms. Cooling slows their activity; it does not sterilise seafood. Temperature affects deterioration rate, while exposure time determines how long that rate acts (Huss, 1995, Chapter 6).

In this example, 5°C gave less than half the shelf life reported at 0°C. A temperature suitable for a general chilled-food requirement is therefore not automatically optimal for quality.

Read the whole history. Deterioration accumulates during exposure; returning a product to cold storage does not undo it. Predictions need a validated model plus information about initial quality, species and packaging. This chart cannot calculate the safety or remaining life of the fictional tuna shipment (Huss, 1995, Chapter 6).

Explore the science in more detail

The delivery mystery

A seafood delivery arrives. The fish is cold, the box looks fine, and the paperwork is complete. Would you accept it?

Before you answer, imagine that this box spent part of its journey waiting on a warm loading dock. It was chilled again before delivery. The thermometer tells us its temperature now. It cannot reconstruct the journey.

Today, we will follow a tuna shipment and see how processors can detect these hidden gaps, protect customers and preserve product quality.

Food Standards Australia New Zealand [FSANZ] (2006, seafood receipt section); Torry Research Station (n.d.).
Where the cold chain can break

The cold chain is the connected system that keeps seafood under appropriate temperature control from harvest through handling, processing, storage and distribution.

Our tuna is chilled onboard, unloaded, received at a processor, cut into portions, packed and dispatched. Temperature control must continue during these operations.

The vulnerable moments are often the handovers: unloading, waiting for inspection, processing delays and loading trucks. Too little ice, equipment faults or slow handling can create warming.

A processor needs both effective cooling and evidence that it worked. A refrigerated truck cannot correct every earlier failure.

FSANZ (2006); U.S. Food and Drug Administration [FDA] (2022, Chapters 7 and 12).
What warming does to seafood

Three processes can reduce seafood quality. Spoilage microorganisms produce unpleasant compounds. The fish’s own enzymes change its tissues after death. Fats can oxidise, causing rancid flavours, especially in fatty fish.

Cooling slows deterioration. It does not reset freshness. Two batches of the same age can therefore have different remaining quality because their temperature histories differ.

Frozen seafood also needs control. During frozen storage, protein changes, oxidation and dehydration can reduce eating quality. A frozen product does not stay high quality indefinitely.

For processors, deteriorating raw material can mean shorter selling time, rejected batches and lower value. Discarding seafood also wastes resources already used to harvest, process and transport it.

For some marine fish, spoilage bacteria convert trimethylamine oxide into trimethylamine, a compound associated with fishy odours. This is a quality mechanism, not a universal test for safety. The initial microbial population, hygiene, species and temperature history all influence deterioration. That is why one shelf-life prediction cannot automatically apply to every seafood product.

During frozen storage, moisture can leave the fish and form frost inside the package as temperatures fluctuate. The product may become drier even without losing total package weight. Stable storage and suitable protective packaging are therefore important.

Huss (1995, Chapter 5); Johnston et al. (1994, Chapter 7); United Nations Environment Programme [UNEP] & Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO] (2022).
Freshness and safety are different

A freshness assessment asks whether the seafood still has acceptable eating quality. A safety assessment asks whether it could cause harm.

Tuna is an important example. Certain bacteria can convert naturally present histidine into histamine. Once formed, histamine is not removed by cooking or freezing.

Other hazards depend on the species, processing and packaging. Reduced-oxygen seafood packaging needs controls for the risk of botulinum toxin formation. Cold-chain monitoring also cannot remove contaminants or naturally occurring marine toxins.

So, neither a normal appearance nor one acceptable temperature reading proves that a batch is safe.

Consider two products from the same factory: chilled tuna portions and a vacuum-packed seafood product. The first needs specific attention to histamine formation. The second requires assessment of reduced-oxygen packaging hazards, including Clostridium botulinum. The species and process still determine the actual hazard analysis. A single generic temperature alarm cannot substitute for that assessment.

FDA (2022, Chapters 3, 6, 7 and 13).
Which temperature should we measure

The air temperature in a cool room and the temperature of seafood are different measurements. Air can warm or cool faster than a packed product. Large fish, cartons and pallet positions can respond differently.

A probe measures temperature at the point where its sensing tip sits. An infrared thermometer mainly measures the surface. Neither automatically represents every fish in a load.

Select measurement locations using temperature mapping: check how temperatures vary across the actual load and process. During cooling, the last part to cool matters. During warming, exposed locations may be important.

Check instruments against a suitable reference, clean and sanitise probes appropriately, and record the batch, location and time. A precise-looking number can still be misleading if the sensor is misplaced.

A room-air alarm is an early warning, while product measurements help determine what the food actually experienced. During initial cooling, the slowest-cooling location may be inside the load. During warming, exposed surfaces can warm first. Sampling and sensor placement must reflect the actual operation rather than convenience.

Check accuracy as well as display resolution: a thermometer showing decimal places is not necessarily accurate. Instruments also need a suitable range and response time. Use temperature mapping and instrument checks to support meaningful records.

Torry Research Station (n.d.); FSANZ (2006, monitoring temperature section).
Compare the monitoring tools

Start with the question each tool can answer.

A handheld probe tells us the temperature at one location and moment. It is useful for receiving checks, but manual readings can miss events between checks.

A data logger stores repeated readings, creating a history for later review. An offline logger is useful when connectivity is unavailable, although someone must retrieve and review its data.

A connected sensor can send readings and alarms through a gateway or mobile network. That can support faster intervention, but only if the connection works and someone responds. Batteries, subscriptions and integration add costs.

A time–temperature indicator, or TTI, changes in response to accumulated exposure. It can make a package’s history easier to interpret. It must be matched to the product and the deterioration process being monitored.

Research has tested TTIs in chilled fish and frozen seafood chains. These studies support their usefulness under evaluated conditions; they do not validate every label for every product.

A freshness indicator works differently: it may respond to compounds produced as fish deteriorates. It measures a proxy for quality rather than simply recording temperature. It must not be treated as a universal safety test.

A TTI works through a temperature-dependent physical, chemical or biological change. The label response needs to correspond sufficiently to the product change of interest under the intended conditions. A visible colour change by itself does not establish this match. Separate quality-validation evidence from safety-validation evidence.

The two cited fish-chain studies provide practical evidence of TTI applications, while also showing that implementation needs evaluation. They support piloting matched systems rather than claiming a universal solution.

Torry Research Station (n.d.); Giannakourou et al. (2005); Tsironi et al. (2016); Zhang et al. (2022). Tool selection and cost comparisons are the group’s qualitative assessment, not vendor quotations.
Would you release this batch

Back to our fictional shipment. At receiving, its measured temperature is two degrees Celsius. But the logger records an earlier excursion to eight degrees for ninety minutes.

Would you release it, chill it again, or place it on hold for assessment? Pause and choose.

The appropriate first response is to hold and assess it using the business’s validated product-specific procedure. These invented numbers alone do not establish safety or determine rejection.

Check the sensor, its location, the full history and the relevant hazard controls. Restore appropriate temperature control, but do not treat rechilling as evidence that the batch is safe. Record the decision and investigate why the excursion occurred.

FDA (2022, Chapter 7); FSANZ (2006, receipt section). The scenario and recommended initial hold are educational judgement; disposition requires the actual food safety plan.
Build a system that leads to action

Our recommendation is a layered system. First, identify hazards for the seafood species, process and packaging. Then establish validated limits and monitoring procedures.

For ordinary non-live chilled seafood, keeping it close to melting-ice temperature is a useful quality objective. Australian guidance generally uses five degrees Celsius or colder for chilled seafood, unless a safe alternative is demonstrated. That is not a universal shelf-life guarantee or a limit for every product.

Next, map the process and choose representative sensors. Link each record to its batch and make someone responsible for reviewing it.

Create an escalation procedure: detect a deviation, verify it, hold affected product, assess the history, document disposition and correct the cause. Set warning alarms early enough to allow intervention before a validated limit is breached.

Finally, test the response through drills and review recurring failures. Recording temperatures is useful only when the business makes decisions from them.

HACCP means Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point. In plain language, identify a significant hazard, determine where it can be controlled, define an acceptable limit, monitor that control and specify action if it fails. A business also needs verification and records. The hazard analysis determines critical control points; every thermometer location is not automatically one.

FSANZ (2006); Torry Research Station (n.d.); FDA (2022, Chapter 2). The layered workflow and warning-alarm recommendation are the group’s proposed implementation.
Better technology with realistic trade-offs

A small processor might begin with calibrated probes, reusable loggers and disciplined review. A larger operation with many routes might justify connected sensors and a shared dashboard. Start with the riskiest handovers rather than buying technology without a defined purpose.

Compare total cost: equipment, calibration, batteries, connectivity, staff time and replacement. Ask whether the system reduces preventable loss or improves response enough to justify that cost.

Future systems could combine temperature histories with validated models of remaining quality. Stock could then be prioritised by earliest predicted expiry, while still respecting safety requirements and approved shelf lives.

Freshness sensors and optical methods may provide additional information, but sensitivity, stability and calibration remain challenges.

Sustainability matters too. Cooling consumes energy and refrigerant leakage can affect climate. Better insulation and efficient refrigeration deserve attention alongside monitoring. Reusable devices need recovery systems; disposable labels add material. Explain indicators clearly to consumers and test whether they understand them before rollout.

For a small site, propose probes plus recoverable loggers and a daily review responsibility. For a larger distributor, pilot connected monitoring on a high-risk route and test signal loss, battery failure and after-hours response. A label system scales by adding labels to packages, but brings recurring purchase and material costs. A reusable system reduces repeated device purchase only when devices are actually recovered.

Estimate benefit using measured baseline losses and response times. Include calibration, staff training, recovery, network fees and maintenance in the cost comparison. Review waste per tonne and energy per tonne alongside safety performance; fewer rejected batches do not justify accepting an unsafe batch.

Zhang et al. (2022); UNEP & FAO (2022); Tsironi et al. (2016). Deployment, lifecycle-cost and consumer-testing proposals are the group’s recommendations, not measured outcomes.

CONTROL MEASURES AND TRADE-OFFS

Monitoring detects. Control acts.

A sensor supplies evidence. Control maintains suitable conditions and manages affected product. A logger cannot cool seafood, and cooling cannot reconstruct a missing history.

Chill and maintain

Use suitable ice or refrigeration throughout handling and processing. Insulation reduces heat gain but does not replace effective cooling.

FSANZ, 2006; FDA, 2022

Prevent warm handovers

Plan unloading and processing to limit uncontrolled waiting; maintain equipment and manage doors and loading practices.

Proposed operational priorities informed by FSANZ, 2006

Keep frozen storage stable

Use appropriate frozen storage and protective packaging. Protein, fat and moisture changes can still reduce quality over time.

Johnston et al., 1994

Respond to deviations

Verify the evidence, identify and hold affected batches, assess under the validated plan, document disposition and correct the cause. Rechilling does not establish safety.

FDA, 2022; proposed workflow

Verify performance

Check instruments, records and the effectiveness of the response. The hazard analysis determines critical control points; every sensor is not automatically a CCP.

FDA, 2022; Torry Research Station, n.d.

Balance resources

Compare energy, refrigerant leakage, equipment maintenance and prevented product loss. Efficient cooling and insulation complement monitoring; resource savings must preserve safety controls.

UNEP & FAO, 2022; proposed evaluation

WHAT THE RESEARCH SHOWS

Promising tools need product-specific proof.

Chilled seabream: a field test

Giannakourou et al. (2005) evaluated enzymatic TTIs on exported gilt-head seabream from harvest to consumption. Label responses at different package positions were compared with recorded temperatures, using validated models of spoilage-bacterial growth.

Finding: the field tests supported TTI usefulness and identified implementation difficulties.

Limit: intermediate microbiological and sensory observations unavailable in the field were obtained in a laboratory replication of the recorded profiles. This supports evaluated conditions; it does not demonstrate universal performance in all fish chains.

Giannakourou et al. (2005). Sensory assessment means checking eating-quality characteristics such as odour or texture.

Frozen seafood: matching matters

Tsironi et al. (2016) evaluated enzymatic and UV-activated photochromic TTIs with frozen blue-shark slices and arrow squid in a production-to-consumption pilot. Predictions of chemical and sensory quality were compared with experimental observations.

Finding: selected, tailored labels adequately monitored quality and shelf life under the evaluated conditions.

Limit: the study concerned particular products, labels and quality models. Applying the approach to another species, package or exposure range requires validation; a quality indicator is not independent proof of pathogen control.

Tsironi et al. (2016). Photochromic describes a light-triggered colour-changing system.
Our interpretation: pilot a matched TTI as an additional quality-information layer. Retain temperature records and the product’s validated safety procedures. Field evidence supports targeted adoption, rather than replacing all controls with a colour label.

REALISTIC RECOMMENDATIONS

Build a system that leads to action.

Start with hazards

Identify the species, process, packaging and intended shelf life. Set validated limits and disposition rules before selecting devices. (FDA, 2022)

Map and measure

Map representative loads; compare air and product readings; verify sensor accuracy and response time. Link location and batch ID to every record. (Torry Research Station, n.d.; FSANZ, 2006)

Make alarms actionable

Assign a responder, verification steps and an out-of-hours escalation route. A detected deviation triggers a product-specific hold and assessment, not automatic release. (FDA, 2022; proposed workflow)

Pilot before expanding

Measure baseline losses, review completeness and response time. Include training, calibration, subscriptions, recovery and maintenance in total cost. These are proposed evaluation steps, not measured outcomes.

Balance resources and quality

Assess waste per tonne and energy per tonne. Efficient refrigeration and insulation complement monitoring; reusable devices require recovery, and disposable labels add materials. (UNEP & FAO, 2022; proposed metrics)

Small site: begin with checked probes, recoverable loggers and an assigned reviewer. Larger network: pilot connected monitoring on high-risk handovers and test loss of signal and after-hours response. Future: validated remaining-quality models may improve stock rotation; they must respect safety requirements and approved shelf lives. Proposed rollout; Zhang et al., 2022; UNEP & FAO, 2022

Choose an upgrade that solves the actual failure

A pilot that measures success

We propose comparing a baseline period with an upgrade on the same product and route, including busy periods and representative loads. Record throughput, initial product condition and relevant handling differences so improvements are not automatically attributed to the device.

Proposed evaluation measures. These are not reported study outcomes or regulatory thresholds.
QuestionMeasureDecision it supports
Is control reliable?Complete batch histories; verified deviations; time from alarm to action; documented dispositionExpand only when records and response meet the food safety plan
Is eating quality preserved?Product-appropriate sensory checks, drip loss or other validated quality measuresConfirm that fewer rejections reflect retained quality
Is it economically feasible?Equipment, calibration, training, staff review, subscriptions, maintenance, recovery and replacement costsCompare annualised ownership cost with verified avoided-loss value; avoid counting the same saving twice
Is it more sustainable?Discarded seafood in kg per tonne; refrigeration kWh per tonne; device/label use and recoveryEvaluate resource changes together, while preserving safety requirements
Do people understand it?Ask operators and customers to interpret normal, changed and unreadable indicatorsImprove wording and instructions before rollout; test whether people wrongly assume the indicator guarantees safety
Stop and investigate if the pilot produces missing histories, unhandled alerts, a mismatch between indicators and validated quality measurements, or unsafe interpretation. Check supplier quotes and actual operating costs before scaling. A favourable financial result never overrides a safety failure.

Future improvements with safeguards

Combining batch identity, temperature history and validated freshness measurements could improve remaining-quality estimates and stock prioritisation. Emerging optical and freshness-sensing approaches still need suitable calibration, specificity and stability (Zhang et al., 2022). We recommend keeping an auditable record, validating performance on the intended products and providing a fallback when data are missing. Pair digital investment with efficient refrigeration, insulation and device recovery rather than assuming more sensors alone reduce emissions (UNEP & FAO, 2022; proposed implementation).

Conclusion

Effective seafood cold-chain monitoring combines reliable temperature records with appropriate cooling and timely corrective action. Processors should identify product-specific hazards, verify sensor performance and review the full temperature history before making decisions. A cold reading at delivery alone does not establish safety. A practical system should protect food safety and quality while considering cost, energy use and product waste (FDA, 2022; FSANZ, 2006; UNEP & FAO, 2022).
